Recode numeric values with Stata-style rules

Source: R/recode.R
stata_recode.Rd

Recode individual values, sets, or closed numeric ranges using ordered rules.

  • stata_recode() (recode()): Keep unmatched values unless .default replaces them, and use named rules to assign value labels.

Usage

stata_recode(x, ..., .default = x)

recode(x, ..., .default = x)

Arguments

x

An integer or double vector, optionally a numeric haven::labelled() vector. Convert integer64 input explicitly before recoding.

...

Two-sided formulas values ~ code, applied in order. Each code is a single number or NA; name a rule to label its code. Expressions use the formula's environment, and stored formulas can be spliced with !!!.

.default

Replacement for unmatched elements: a single number, NA, or a vector as long as x. By default, keep the input values after SPSS user-missing codes have been converted to NA.

Value

An integer or double vector with the length and order of x. Named rules produce a haven::labelled() vector; otherwise the result is numeric without value labels. Names and the variable label are kept; previous value labels, SPSS missing-value metadata, and other input attributes are dropped. See Details for integer preservation.

Details

Output type

Integer input stays integer when every code and .default is a whole number within integer range, so 1:5 ~ 1 does not promote it to double. Double input stays double. Fractions, out-of-range numbers, infinities, NaN, and tagged missing codes or defaults require double output; ordinary NA does not promote integer input. The input is not modified.

Matching

The left side of each rule is read before evaluation:

  • a:b selects the closed range a <= x <= b, including decimals, like Stata's a/b. Thus 1:5 matches 4.5, rather than enumerating integers. Bounds must be single non-missing numbers, with the lower bound no greater than the upper bound. lo:hi uses the formula's environment.

  • c(...) combines values and ranges, for example c(1, 3:5).

  • Other expressions are evaluated as value sets. Non-missing values match exactly; a missing value in a set matches every missing type, as below.

Rules match the input before any replacements, after SPSS missing-value conversion. The first matching rule wins, so 1 ~ 2, 2 ~ 1 swaps the codes. Supply .default to replace all unmatched elements, including missing ones.

On the left side, bare min and max mean -Inf and Inf. Unlike Stata's keywords, they do not refer to observed extrema: min:min does not select the smallest observed code. Calls such as min(x) still evaluate normally. Bounds, like value sets, must be ordinary integer or double numbers; convert classed numbers such as integer64 explicitly.

Missing values and labels

NA ~ code matches NA, NaN, and all tagged missing values, like Stata's missing keyword. The same applies to any missing selector: for example, haven::tagged_na("a") ~ 0 also replaces other tags and ordinary NA. Individual missing types cannot be selected separately. Unmatched tagged missing values keep their tags when .default is omitted.

SPSS user-missing codes and ranges become NA before matching, so their stored codes cannot be selected as ordinary numbers. Old value labels are removed even when no values change. Named rules supply new labels, which are kept even if their codes are unobserved. A code cannot have two labels, a label cannot name two codes, and a missing code cannot be labelled.

Stata and other R functions

Use dplyr::mutate() to replace a variable or create a new one, as with Stata's generate() option. Use dplyr::across() to apply rules to several variables. Common rule translations are:

Stata ruleR rule or argument
(1/5 = 1)1:5 ~ 1
(1 3 7 = 0)c(1, 3, 7) ~ 0
(9 = .)9 ~ NA
(missing = 0)NA ~ 0
(else = .).default = NA
(1/5 = 1 "Low")Low = 1:5 ~ 1

Like Stata's recode, these functions operate on numeric values. For text, use dplyr::recode_values() or dplyr::replace_values() in dplyr 1.2.0 and later, or dplyr::case_match() with older versions. For factors, use forcats::fct_recode() or forcats::fct_collapse().

The alias recode() shares its name with dplyr::recode(). Whichever package is attached last masks the other. Prefer stata_recode() or an explicit namespace to avoid attach-order ambiguity.

See also

Other variable generation functions: as_dummy(), cut_quantile(), panel, row_egen, std()

Examples

# Keep unmatched values
x <- c(1, 4.5, 6, 9, 12, NA)
stata_recode(x, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2)
#> [1]  1  1  2  2 12 NA

# Replace unmatched values with missing
stata_recode(x, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2, .default = NA)
#> [1]  1  1  2  2 NA NA

# Unbounded intervals and missing values
stata_recode(x, min:5 ~ 0, 6:max ~ 1, NA ~ 9)
#> [1] 0 0 1 1 1 9

# Swap codes without cascading replacements
stata_recode(c(1, 2, 3), 1 ~ 2, 2 ~ 1)
#> [1] 2 1 3

# Assign new value labels
stata_recode(x, Low = 1:5 ~ 1, High = 6:max ~ 2)
#> <labelled<double>[6]>
#> [1]  1  1  2  2  2 NA
#> 
#> Labels:
#>  value label
#>      1   Low
#>      2  High

# Create a new variable
d <- data.frame(score = c(2, 7, 11))
dplyr::mutate(
  d,
  group = stata_recode(score, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2, .default = NA)
)
#>   score group
#> 1     2     1
#> 2     7     2
#> 3    11    NA

# Apply rules to several variables and prefix the new names
items <- data.frame(item1 = c(1, 7, 9), item2 = c(3, 8, 12))
dplyr::mutate(
  items,
  dplyr::across(
    dplyr::everything(),
    function(v) stata_recode(v, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2, 11:15 ~ 3),
    .names = "r_{.col}"
  )
)
#>   item1 item2 r_item1 r_item2
#> 1     1     3       1       1
#> 2     7     8       2       2
#> 3     9    12       2       3
